But we must let it continue hanging there a while till we can get a chance to attend to it. For the present other matters press, and the best we can do now for the head, is to pray heaven the tackles may hold.

Now, during the past night and forenoon, the Pequod had gradually drifted into a sea, which, by its occasional patches of yellow brit, gave unusual tokens of the vicinity of Right Whales, a species of the Leviathan that but few supposed to be at this particular time lurking anywhere near. And though all hands commonly disdained the capture of those inferior creatures; and though the Pequod was not commissioned to cruise for them at all, and though she had passed numbers of them near the Crozetts without lowering a boat; yet now that a Sperm Whale had been brought alongside and beheaded, to the surprise of all, the announcement was made that a Right Whale should be captured that day, if opportunity offered.

Nor was this long wanting. Tall spouts were seen to leeward; and two boats, Stubb’s and Flask’s, were detached in pursuit. Pulling further and further away, they at last became almost invisible to the men at the mast-head. But suddenly in the distance, they saw a great heap of tumultuous white water, and soon after news came from aloft that one or both the boats must be fast. An interval passed and the boats were in plain sight, in the act of being dragged right towards the ship by the towing whale. So close did the monster come to the hull, that at first it seemed as if he meant it malice; but suddenly going down in a maelstrom, within three rods of the planks, he wholly disappeared from view, as if diving under the keel. “Cut, cut!” was the cry from the ship to the boats, which, for one instant, seemed on the point of being brought with a deadly dash against the vessel’s side. But having plenty of line yet in the tubs, and the whale not sounding very rapidly, they paid out abundance of rope, and at the same time pulled with all their might so as to get ahead of the ship. For a few minutes the struggle was intensely critical; for while they still slacked out the tightened line in one direction, and still plied their oars in another, the contending strain threatened to take them under. But it was only a few feet advance they sought to gain. And they stuck to it till they did gain it; when instantly, a swift tremor was felt running like lightning along the keel, as the strained line, scraping beneath the ship, suddenly rose to view under her bows, snapping and quivering; and so flinging off its drippings, that the drops fell like bits of broken glass on the water, while the whale beyond also rose to sight, and once more the boats were free to fly. But the fagged whale abated his speed, and blindly altering his course, went round the stern of the ship towing the two boats after him, so that they performed a complete circuit.

Meantime, they hauled more and more upon their lines, till close flanking him on both sides, Stubb answered Flask with lance for lance; and thus round and round the Pequod the battle went, while the multitudes of sharks that had before swum round the Sperm Whale’s body, rushed to the fresh blood that was spilled, thirstily drinking at every new gash, as the eager Israelites did at the new bursting fountains that poured from the smitten rock.
At last his spout grew thick, and with a frightful roll and vomit, he turned upon his back a corpse.
While the two headsmen were engaged in making fast cords to his flukes, and in other ways getting the mass in readiness for towing, some conversation ensued between them.
“I wonder what the old man wants with this lump of foul lard,” said Stubb, not without some disgust at the thought of having to do with so ignoble a leviathan.

“Wants with it?” said Flask, coiling some spare line in the boat’s bow, “did you never hear that the ship which but once has a Sperm Whale’s head hoisted on her starboard side, and at the same time a Right Whale’s on the larboard; did you never hear, Stubb, that that ship can never afterwards capsize?”
“Why not?

“I don’t know, but I heard that gamboge ghost of a Fedallah saying so, and he seems to know all about ships’ charms. But I sometimes think he’ll charm the ship to no good at last. I don’t half like that chap, Stubb. Did you ever notice how that tusk of his is a sort of carved into a snake’s head, Stubb?”

“Sink him! I never look at him at all; but if ever I get a chance of a dark night, and he standing hard by the bulwarks, and no one by; look down there, Flask”—pointing into the sea with a peculiar motion of both hands—“Aye, will I! Flask, I take that Fedallah to be the devil in disguise. Do you believe that cock and bull story about his having been stowed away on board ship? He’s the devil, I say. The reason why you don’t see his tail, is because he tucks it up out of sight; he carries it coiled away in his pocket, I guess. Blast him! now that I think of it, he’s always wanting oakum to stuff into the toes of his boots.”
“He sleeps in his boots, don’t he? He hasn’t got any hammock; but I’ve seen him lay of nights in a coil of rigging.”
“No doubt, and it’s because of his cursed tail; he coils it down, do ye see, in the eye of the rigging.”
“What’s the old man have so much to do with him for?”
“Striking up a swap or a bargain, I suppose.”
“Bargain?—about what?”

“Why, do ye see, the old man is hard bent after that White Whale, and the devil there is trying to come round him, and get him to swap away his silver watch, or his soul, or something of that sort, and then he’ll surrender Moby Dick.”
“Pooh! Stubb, you are skylarking; how can Fedallah do that?”

“I don’t know, Flask, but the devil is a curious chap, and a wicked one, I tell ye. Why, they say as how he went a sauntering into the old flag-ship once, switching his tail about devilish easy and gentlemanlike, and inquiring if the old governor was at home. Well, he was at home, and asked the devil what he wanted. The devil, switching his hoofs, up and says, ‘I want John.’ ‘What for?’ says the old governor. ‘What business is that of yours,’ says the devil, getting mad,—‘I want to use him.’ ‘Take him,’ says the governor—and by the Lord, Flask, if the devil didn’t give John the Asiatic cholera before he got through with him, I’ll eat this whale in one mouthful. But look sharp—ain’t you all ready there? Well, then, pull ahead, and let’s get the whale alongside.”
“I think I remember some such story as you were telling,” said Flask, when at last the two boats were slowly advancing with their burden towards the ship, “but I can’t remember where.”
“Three Spaniards? Adventures of those three bloody-minded soldadoes? Did ye read it there, Flask? I guess ye did?”
“No: never saw such a book; heard of it, though. But now, tell me, Stubb, do you suppose that that devil you was speaking of just now, was the same you say is now on board the Pequod?”

“Am I the same man that helped kill this whale? Doesn’t the devil live for ever; who ever heard that the devil was dead? Did you ever see any parson a wearing mourning for the devil? And if the devil has a latch-key to get into the admiral’s cabin, don’t you suppose he can crawl into a porthole? Tell me that, Mr. Flask?”
“How old do you suppose Fedallah is, Stubb?”

“Do you see that mainmast there?” pointing to the ship; “well, that’s the figure one; now take all the hoops in the Pequod’s hold, and string along in a row with that mast, for oughts, do you see; well, that wouldn’t begin to be Fedallah’s age. Nor all the coopers in creation couldn’t show hoops enough to make oughts enough.”

“But see here, Stubb, I thought you a little boasted just now, that you meant to give Fedallah a sea-toss, if you got a good chance. Now, if he’s so old as all those hoops of yours come to, and if he is going to live for ever, what good will it do to pitch him overboard—tell me that?
“Give him a good ducking, anyhow.”
“But he’d crawl back.”
“Duck him again; and keep ducking him.”
“Suppose he should take it into his head to duck you, though—yes, and drown you—what then?”

“I should like to see him try it; I’d give him such a pair of black eyes that he wouldn’t dare to show his face in the admiral’s cabin again for a long while, let alone down in the orlop there, where he lives, and hereabouts on the upper decks where he sneaks so much. Damn the devil, Flask; so you suppose I’m afraid of the devil? Who’s afraid of him, except the old governor who daresn’t catch him and put him in double-darbies, as he deserves, but lets him go about kidnapping people; aye, and signed a bond with him, that all the people the devil kidnapped, he’d roast for him? There’s a governor!”
“Do you suppose Fedallah wants to kidnap Captain Ahab?”

“Do I suppose it? You’ll know it before long, Flask. But I am going now to keep a sharp look-out on him; and if I see anything very suspicious going on, I’ll just take him by the nape of his neck, and say—Look here, Beelzebub, you don’t do it; and if he makes any fuss, by the Lord I’ll make a grab into his pocket for his tail, take it to the capstan, and give him such a wrenching and heaving, that his tail will come short off at the stump—do you see; and then, I rather guess when he finds himself docked in that queer fashion, he’ll sneak off without the poor satisfaction of feeling his tail between his legs.”
“And what will you do with the tail, Stubb?”
“Do with it? Sell it for an ox whip when we get home;—what else?”
“Now, do you mean what you say, and have been saying all along, Stubb?”
“Mean or not mean, here we are at the ship.”
The boats were here hailed, to tow the whale on the larboard side, where fluke chains and other necessaries were already prepared for securing him.
“Didn’t I tell you so?” said Flask; “yes, you’ll soon see this right whale’s head hoisted up opposite that parmacetti’s.”

In good time, Flask’s saying proved true. As before, the Pequod steeply leaned over towards the sperm whale’s head, now, by the counterpoise of both heads, she regained her even keel; though sorely strained, you may well believe. So, when on one side you hoist in Locke’s head, you go over that way; but now, on the other side, hoist in Kant’s and you come back again; but in very poor plight. Thus, some minds for ever keep trimming boat. Oh, ye foolish! throw all these thunder-heads overboard, and then you will float light and right.

In disposing of the body of a right whale, when brought alongside the ship, the same preliminary proceedings commonly take place as in the case of a sperm whale; only, in the latter instance, the head is cut off whole, but in the former the lips and tongue are separately removed and hoisted on deck, with all the well known black bone attached to what is called the crown-piece. But nothing like this, in the present case, had been done. The carcases of both whales had dropped astern; and the head-laden ship not a little resembled a mule carrying a pair of overburdening panniers.

Meantime, Fedallah was calmly eyeing the right whale’s head, and ever and anon glancing from the deep wrinkles there to the lines in his own hand. And Ahab chanced so to stand, that the Parsee occupied his shadow; while, if the Parsee’s shadow was there at all it seemed only to blend with, and lengthen Ahab’s. As the crew toiled on, Laplandish speculations were bandied among them, concerning all these passing things.

"How old do you suppose Fedallah is, Stubb?"

"Do you see that mainmast there?" pointing to the ship. "Well, that's the figure one. Now take all the hoops in the Pequod's hold, and string them along in a row with that mast, for zeros, do you see? Well, that wouldn't even begin to be Fedallah's age. Not all the coopers in creation could show hoops enough to make zeros enough."

"But see here, Stubb, I thought you boasted a little just now that you meant to give Fedallah a toss in the sea if you got a good chance. Now, if he's as old as all those hoops of yours come to, and if he's going to live forever, what good will it do to pitch him overboard — tell me that?"
"Give him a good ducking, anyway."
"But he'd crawl back."
"Duck him again, and keep ducking him."
"Suppose he should take it into his head to duck you, though — yes, and drown you — what then?"

"I'd like to see him try it. I'd give him such a pair of black eyes he wouldn't dare show his face in the admiral's cabin again for a good long while, let alone down in the orlop there, where he lives, or around here on the upper decks, where he sneaks about so much. Damn the devil, Flask — so you think I'm afraid of the devil? Who's afraid of him, except the old governor, who doesn't dare catch him and clap him in double-darbies — double handcuffs — as he deserves, but lets him go around kidnapping people? Yes, and he even signed a bond with him that he'd roast for him all the people the devil kidnapped. There's a governor for you!"
"Do you suppose Fedallah wants to kidnap Captain Ahab?"

"Do I think so? You'll find out before long, Flask. But from now on I'm going to keep a sharp lookout on him, and if I see anything very suspicious going on, I'll just grab him by the scruff of the neck and say — Look here, Beelzebub, don't you do it. And if he makes any fuss, by the Lord, I'll reach into his pocket for his tail, take it to the capstan, and give it such a wrench and heave that it snaps clean off at the stump — do you see? And then, I rather guess, when he finds himself docked in that odd way, he'll slink off without even the poor satisfaction of feeling his tail between his legs."
"And what will you do with the tail, Stubb?"
"Do with it? Sell it for an ox whip when we get home — what else?"
"Now, do you mean what you say, and have been saying all along, Stubb?"
"Mean or not mean, here we are at the ship."
The boats were now hailed to tow the whale on the port side, where fluke chains and other gear were already prepared for securing him.
"Didn't I tell you so?" said Flask. "Yes, you'll soon see this right whale's head hoisted up opposite that sperm whale's."

In good time, Flask's saying proved true. As before, the Pequod had leaned steeply over toward the sperm whale's head; now, by the counterweight of both heads, she regained her even keel — though sorely strained, you may well believe. So, when on one side you hoist in Locke's head, you go over that way; but now, on the other side, hoist in Kant's and you come back again — but in very poor shape. Thus some minds forever keep trimming boat. Oh, you foolish ones! Throw all these thunder-heads overboard, and then you will float light and right.

When the body of a right whale is brought alongside the ship to be dealt with, the same preliminary steps usually take place as with a sperm whale; the difference is that the sperm whale's head is cut off whole, whereas the right whale's lips and tongue are removed separately and hoisted on deck, together with all the familiar black bone (the baleen, or whalebone) attached to what is called the crown-piece. But in this case nothing of the kind had been done. Both carcasses had drifted astern, and the ship, weighed down with heads, looked rather like a mule carrying a pair of overloaded panniers.

Meanwhile, Fedallah was calmly eyeing the right whale's head, and every now and then glancing from the deep wrinkles there to the lines in his own hand. And Ahab happened to stand so that the Parsee occupied his shadow; while, if the Parsee's shadow was there at all, it seemed only to blend with and lengthen Ahab's. As the crew toiled on, Laplandish speculations were bandied about among them concerning all these passing things.

modern_da.title: Kapitel 73 — Stubb og Flask dræber en rethval; og fører så en samtale
paragraphs: over Ham.

Husk, at en kaskelots enorme hoved hele tiden har hængt fra Pequods side. Men vi må lade det hænge der lidt længere, til vi får lejlighed til at tage os af det. Andre ting haster nu, og det bedste, vi for tiden kan gøre for hovedet, er at bede himlen om, at taljerne holder.

I løbet af natten og morgenen var Pequod nu efterhånden drevet ind i et hav, som ved sine pletvise bælter af gul brit gav usædvanlige tegn på, at der var rethvaler i nærheden — en art af leviatan, som få troede lurede noget sted i nærheden på dette tidspunkt. Og selv om alle mand sædvanligvis foragtede fangsten af disse ringere væsner, og selv om Pequod slet ikke havde fået til opgave at krydse efter dem, og selv om hun var sejlet forbi masser af dem ved Crozet-øerne uden at sænke en båd — så blev der nu, hvor en kaskelot var bragt ind langs skibet og havde fået hovedet skåret af, til alles overraskelse meddelt, at en rethval skulle fanges den dag, hvis lejligheden bød sig.

Vi behøvede ikke vente længe. Høje sprøjt blev set i læ, og to både, Stubbs og Flasks, blev sendt efter dem. De roede længere og længere væk, til folkene i mastetoppen næppe kunne se dem. Så så de pludselig langt borte en stor dynge oprørt hvidt vand, og snart kom der besked ned fra oven, at en af bådene eller begge måtte være fast. Efter en stund kom bådene klart til syne, trukket lige mod skibet af hvalen, som havde dem på slæb. Uhyret kom så tæt på skroget, at det først så ud, som om han ville det ondt; men så, inden for tre stænger fra plankerne, dykkede han pludselig ned i en hvirvel og forsvandt helt, som om han dykkede ind under kølen. »Kap, kap!« råbte skibet til bådene, som et øjeblik så ud til helt sikkert at ville blive smadret mod skibssiden. Men da de stadig havde masser af line i tubberne, og hvalen ikke dykkede særlig hurtigt, gav de frit rebet ud, mens de roede af alle kræfter for at komme foran skibet. I nogle minutter var det yderst kritisk: Mens de gav den spændte line ud i den ene retning og arbejdede med årerne i en anden, truede de modsatte træk med at trække dem under. Men alt, hvad de behøvede at vinde, var nogle få fod. De blev ved, til de fik dem. I det samme løb et hurtigt sitren som et lyn langs kølen: Den anstrengte line, der skrabede under skibet, dukkede pludselig op under bovene, knækkende og dirrende og rystende dryppene af sig, så de faldt som stumper af knust glas på vandet. Hvalen kom også til syne længere væk, og endnu en gang var bådene frie til at flyve af sted. Men den udmattede hval sænkede farten og, blindt skiftende kurs, svingede den rundt om skibets hæk med de to både på slæb, så de beskrev en hel cirkel.

Imens halede de mere og mere ind på deres liner, indtil Stubb, tæt langs ham på begge sider, svarede Flask lanse for lanse; og sådan gik kampen rundt og rundt om Pequod, mens de mange hajer, der havde svømmet rundt om kaskelottens krop, styrtede hen til det friske blod, der blev spildt, og tørstigt drak af hvert nyt sår, som de ivrige israelitter drak af de nye kilder, der brød frem af den slåede klippe.
Til sidst blev hans sprøjt tykt, og med en gyselig rullen og et opkast væltede han om på ryggen, et lig.
Mens de to styrmænd var optaget af at binde snore om hans halevinger og ellers gøre den store masse klar til slæb, kom de to i samtale.
»Jeg undrer mig over, hvad den gamle vil med den her klump stinkende fedt,« sagde Stubb, noget væmmet ved tanken om at skulle have med sådan en ussel leviatan at gøre.

»Hvad han vil med den?« sagde Flask, mens han lagde noget ekstra line op i bådens forstavn. »Har du aldrig hørt, at det skib, der bare én gang har haft et kaskelothoved hejst op på styrbord side og samtidig et rethvalhoved på bagbord — har du aldrig hørt, Stubb, at sådan et skib aldrig siden kan kæntre?«
»Hvorfor ikke?«

»Det ved jeg ikke, men jeg hørte det gullige spøgelse Fedallah sige det, og han ser ud til at vide alt om skibes lykkebringere. Men jeg tror nogle gange, at han i sidste ende kommer til at fortrylle skibet til ulykke. Jeg bryder mig ikke om den fyr, Stubb. Har du lagt mærke til, at hans stødtand er skåret ud som et slangehoved, Stubb?«

»Pokker tage ham! Jeg ser slet ikke på ham. Men hvis jeg nogensinde får chancen en mørk nat, hvor han står tæt ved essingen og ingen er i nærheden — se derned, Flask« — og han pegede ud over havet med en ejendommelig bevægelse med begge hænder — »ja, det gør jeg! Flask, jeg tager Fedallah for fanden selv i forklædning. Tror du på den røverhistorie om, at han er gemt væk om bord som blind passager? Han er fanden, siger jeg dig. Grunden til, at man ikke ser hans hale, er, at han stikker den op, så den ikke kan ses; han går vist rundt med den sammenrullet i lommen. Forbandet være han! Nu jeg tænker på det, beder han altid om værg til at stoppe i tæerne på sine støvler.«
»Han sover i støvlerne, ikke? Han har ingen hængekøje, men jeg har set ham ligge om natten i en bunke tovværk.«
»Det er der ingen tvivl om — og det er på grund af hans forbandede hale. Han lægger den sammenrullet, ser du, i øjet på rigningen.«
»Hvad har den gamle egentlig så meget med ham at gøre?«
»Slår vel et bytte eller en handel af, kan jeg tænke mig.«
»En handel? — om hvad?«

»Jamen, ser du, den gamle er helt opslugt af den hvide hval, og fanden dér prøver at komme ind på ham og få ham til at bytte sit sølvur bort, eller sin sjæl, eller noget i den stil, og så vil han aflevere Moby Dick.«
»Sludder! Stubb, du laver sjov. Hvordan skulle Fedallah kunne det?«

»Det ved jeg ikke, Flask, men fanden er en underlig en, og en ond en, siger jeg dig. Der fortælles jo, at han engang kom slentrende ind i det gamle admiralskib og svingede med halen, så djævelsk adstadigt og herremandsagtigt, og spurgte, om den gamle guvernør var hjemme. Jo, han var hjemme og spurgte fanden, hvad han ville. Fanden svingede med hovene og sagde: ›Jeg vil have John.‹ ›Hvad skal du med ham?‹ sagde den gamle guvernør. ›Hvad rager det dig?‹ sagde fanden og blev gal i hovedet — ›jeg skal bruge ham.‹ ›Tag ham bare,‹ sagde guvernøren — og ved Gud, Flask, hvis ikke fanden gav John asiatisk kolera, før han var færdig med ham, skal jeg æde denne hval i én mundfuld. Men pas nu på — er I ikke klar derovre? Nå, så træk for fuld kraft, så får vi hvalen op langs skibet.«
»Jeg synes, jeg husker en historie, der minder om den, du fortalte,« sagde Flask, da de to både endelig langsomt nærmede sig skibet med deres byrde. »Men jeg kan ikke huske, hvor jeg har hørt den.«
»De tre spaniere? Eventyrene for de tre blodtørstige soldater? Har du læst den dér, Flask? Det har du vist?«
»Nej — jeg har aldrig set sådan en bog. Jeg har dog hørt om den. Men sig mig nu, Stubb — tror du, at den fanden, du talte om lige før, er den samme, som du siger er om bord på Pequod nu?«

»Er jeg den samme mand, som var med til at dræbe denne hval? Lever fanden ikke evigt? Hvem har nogensinde hørt om, at fanden døde? Har du nogensinde set en præst gå i sorg over fanden? Og hvis fanden har en dørnøgle, så han kan lukke sig selv ind i admiralens kahyt, tror du så ikke, han kan kravle gennem en koøje? Svar mig på det, Mr. Flask!«
»Hvor gammel tror du, Fedallah er, Stubb?«

»Ser du den stormast dér?« og han pegede på skibet. »Se, den er tallet ét. Tag nu alle tøndebånd i Pequods lastrum og træk dem op på række ved siden af masten, som nuller, ser du? Nå, så ville det ikke engang begynde at nå op på Fedallahs alder. Ikke alle bødkere i hele verden kunne skaffe bånd nok til at lave nuller nok.«

»Men hør nu her, Stubb, jeg syntes, du pralede lidt lige før med, at du ville give Fedallah et skub i havet, hvis du fik en god chance. Men hvis han er så gammel, som alle dine bånd tilsammen kommer til, og hvis han skal leve evigt, hvad nytter det så at smide ham overbord — sig mig det!«
»Give ham en ordentlig dukkert, i hvert fald.«
»Men han ville kravle op igen.«
»Dukke ham igen, og blive ved med at dukke ham.«
»Men hvis han nu fik det indfald at dukke dig — ja, og drukne dig — hvad så?«

»Det skulle jeg da gerne se ham prøve. Jeg ville give ham sådan et par blå øjne, at han ikke ville turde vise sit ansigt i admiralens kahyt igen i meget lang tid, endsige dernede i underdækket, hvor han bor, eller heromkring på de øvre dæk, hvor han sniger sig så meget rundt. Pokker tage fanden, Flask — så du tror, jeg er bange for fanden? Hvem er bange for ham, undtagen den gamle guvernør, som ikke tør fange ham og lægge ham i dobbelte jern — dobbelte håndjern — som han fortjener, men lader ham gå rundt og kidnappe folk? Ja, og han har endda skrevet under på en kontrakt med ham om, at han vil stege alle de mennesker for ham, som fanden har kidnappet. Sikken en guvernør!«
»Tror du, at Fedallah vil kidnappe kaptajn Ahab?«

»Om jeg tror det? Det finder du ud af før eller siden, Flask. Men fra nu af vil jeg holde skarpt udkig efter ham, og hvis jeg ser noget, der virker rigtig mistænkeligt, tager jeg ham bare i nakkeskindet og siger — Hør her, Beelzebub, det gør du ikke. Og hvis han laver ballade, ved Gud, så rækker jeg ned i hans lomme efter hans hale, tager den med hen til ankerspillet og giver den sådan et ryk og et hiv, at den knækker lige ved roden — forstår du? Og så, gætter jeg på, når han finder sig selv kuperet på den mærkelige måde, vil han liste af uden så meget som den ringe tilfredsstilling at mærke sin hale mellem benene.«
»Og hvad vil du gøre med halen, Stubb?«
»Gøre med den? Sælge den som oksepisk, når vi kommer hjem — hvad ellers?«
»Mener du nu, hvad du siger, og hvad du har sagt hele tiden, Stubb?«
»Mener eller ikke mener, nu er vi ved skibet.«
Bådene blev nu råbt an om at slæbe hvalen til bagbord, hvor halekæderne og andet grej allerede lå klar til at gøre den fast.
»Sagde jeg ikke det?« sagde Flask. »Ja, du skal snart se denne rethvals hoved blive hejst op over for kaskelottens.«

Med tiden viste Flasks ord sig at holde stik. Som før havde Pequod hældet stejlt over mod kaskelottens hoved; nu, ved de to hoveders modvægt, rejste hun sig til en lige køl — omend svært anstrengt, som du nok kan forestille dig. Så når man på den ene side hejser Lockes hoved ind, går man over til den side; men hejser man nu på den anden side Kants ind, kommer man tilbage igen — men i meget dårlig stand. Sådan holder visse hoveder altid på med at trimme båden. Åh, I tåber! Smid alle disse tordenskyer overbord, så vil I flyde let og rigtigt.

Når en rethvals krop bringes langs skibet for at blive behandlet, foregår de samme indledende skridt som regel som med en kaskelot; forskellen er, at kaskelottens hoved skæres af i ét stykke, mens rethvalens læber og tunge fjernes hver for sig og hejses op på dækket, sammen med alle de velkendte sorte barder (baleen, eller hvalben), der sidder fast på det, der kaldes kronestykket. Men i dette tilfælde var intet af den slags blevet gjort. Begge kroppe var drevet agterud, og skibet, tynget ned af hoveder, lignede snarere et muldyr med et par overlæssede kurve.

Imens betragtede Fedallah roligt rethvalens hoved og lod nu og da blikket gå fra de dybe rynker dér til linjerne i sin egen hånd. Og Ahab kom til at stå sådan, at parsien befandt sig i hans skygge; og hvis parsiens skygge overhovedet var der, syntes den kun at smelte sammen med Ahabs og forlænge den. Mens mandskabet slæbte videre, blev der blandt dem kastet rundt med lapske gisninger om alle disse forbipasserende ting.
